checklist.element: Leg-to-beam bolt and gusset, each frame
checklist.confirm: Bolt size (1/2", 8-15/16" grip), edge and end distances in the legs and beam, washers on the tilted outer faces, and that the gusset and bolt together carry the beam's reaction.
checklist.why: Each frame carries half of every swing load into the legs through this joint; connections are not computed.

checklist.confirm: That each frame holds the beam against rolling over at its support.
checklist.why: The beam stability factor assumes it; without that restraint the beam can buckle sideways at a lower load.

checklist.confirm: That the frames resist side-to-side and front-to-back swing forces without racking, and whether corner braces are needed.
checklist.why: Swinging pushes the top of the frame back and forth; racking is not computed.

checklist.confirm: Burial depth (24"), soil, what each leg's end stands on (gravel or tamped soil), whether the backfill or concrete around it sheds water away from the wood, and lumber rated for ground contact (UC4A, or UC4B if critical or hard to replace).
checklist.why: Burial keeps the frame from lifting and walking; tipping and anchoring are not computed.

checklist.confirm: Hangers rated for swing use, installed through the beam as the manufacturer specifies, with holes no larger than the bending check takes.
checklist.why: The hanger margin uses the manufacturer's rating, which holds only for its specified installation.

checklist.confirm: Boards free of large knots near the edges (especially near midspan of the beam), steep grain slope, splits, and wane.
checklist.why: Design values assume the grade; a defect in the wrong place lowers strength more than the grade allows for.

checklist.confirm: An inspection routine: nuts and bolts twice a month, seats and chains monthly (CPSC Pub. 324, p. 5), and decay at the ground line.
checklist.why: Wood shrinks and bolts loosen, especially in pressure-treated lumber that was sold wet.

steps.title: Treat every cut with preservative

method.name: Brushed on
setup: Use the preservative on the shopping list, made for treating cuts in treated wood, and read its label for how to apply it and how long to let it dry.
technique: Brush the sawdust off each cut.
Brush the preservative onto each of the 2 cuts on the piece, and onto any corner you rounded or chamfered, until the wood stops soaking it in.
Add a second coat if the label calls for one.
Wipe off what has not soaked in.
Treat 1 this way.
mistakes: Leaving a cut bare because it will not show, such as the foot of a leg, leaves wood the treatment may never have reached. Coat every cut.
Bolting a part in place before its cuts are treated hides faces you can no longer reach. Treat every cut first.

safety.text: Read the precautions on the preservative’s label before you open it, and follow them: the label says what to wear and where to work.

steps.title: Treat every cut with preservative

method.name: Brushed on
setup: Use the preservative on the shopping list, made for treating cuts in treated wood, and read its label for how to apply it and how long to let it dry.
technique: Brush the sawdust off each cut.
Brush the preservative onto each of the 2 cuts on the piece, and onto any corner you rounded or chamfered, until the wood stops soaking it in.
Add a second coat if the label calls for one.
Wipe off what has not soaked in.
Treat 1 this way.
mistakes: Leaving a cut bare because it will not show, such as the foot of a leg, leaves wood the treatment may never have reached. Coat every cut.
Bolting a part in place before its cuts are treated hides faces you can no longer reach. Treat every cut first.

safety.text: Read the precautions on the preservative’s label before you open it, and follow them: the label says what to wear and where to work.

steps.title: Dig the leg holes

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder to look over the structural checks and the checklist, with the margins and assumptions they list.
flags.why: A part that breaks, sags, or tips under a person can hurt them, and Kerf checks only part of what holds a structure up.

steps.title: Bolt the crossbars and gussets across the legs

method.name: With a spade bit, from one side
setup: Clamp the parts together in their positions from the plan.
Chuck a 9/16" bit, for the 1/2" bolts, with an extension if the bit alone does not reach 5".
technique: Mark each hole center from the cut detail on the face you drill from.
Start the bit at low speed so its point does not wander, then drill square to the face, 5" through every part.
Back the bit out often to clear the chips. A spade bit does not pull them out on its own.
Drill 8 holes this way.
mistakes: Unclamping the parts before every hole is drilled lets them shift, so later holes do not line up. Drill all the holes in a joint before you unclamp it.
Pushing the bit out through the far face tears out the wood around the hole. Slow down as the point comes through, and finish from the far side if it splinters.

safety.text: Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.
Unplug the tool, or take out its battery, before you change a blade or bit.
Drill 9/16" for a 1/2" bolt. A hole a little larger than the bolt lets it go in without being driven.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

method.name: Brushed in
setup: Use the preservative on the shopping list, made for treating cuts in treated wood, and read its label for how to apply it and how long to let it dry.
technique: Brush or blow the chips out of each hole.

Wet a brush narrow enough for a 9/16" hole, or a rag wrapped on a thin stick, with the preservative, and work it through the 5" of the hole from one face, then from the other, so the whole inside is wet.
Wipe off what runs out onto the faces.
Treat 8 holes this way, then put in the bolts once the label says it has soaked in.
mistakes: Coating only the ends of a hole leaves bare wood in the middle, where the parts meet. Work the brush through from both faces.

steps.title: Drill the swing hanger holes in the beam

method.name: With a spade bit, from one side
setup: Clamp the parts together in their positions from the plan.
Chuck a 9/16" bit, for the 1/2" bolts, with an extension if the bit alone does not reach 5-1/2".
technique: Mark each hole center from the cut detail on the face you drill from.
Start the bit at low speed so its point does not wander, then drill square to the face, 5-1/2" through every part.
Back the bit out often to clear the chips. A spade bit does not pull them out on its own.
Drill 4 holes this way.
mistakes: Unclamping the parts before every hole is drilled lets them shift, so later holes do not line up. Drill all the holes in a joint before you unclamp it.
Pushing the bit out through the far face tears out the wood around the hole. Slow down as the point comes through, and finish from the far side if it splinters.

safety.text: Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.
Unplug the tool, or take out its battery, before you change a blade or bit.
Drill 9/16" for a 1/2" bolt. A hole a little larger than the bolt lets it go in without being driven.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

checklist.confirm: Bolt size (1/2", 8-15/16" grip), edge and end distances in the legs and beam, washers on the tilted outer faces, and that the gusset and bolt together carry the beam's reaction.
checklist.why: Each frame carries half of every swing load into the legs through this joint; connections are not computed.

checklist.confirm: That each frame holds the beam against rolling over at its support.
checklist.why: The beam stability factor assumes it; without that restraint the beam can buckle sideways at a lower load.

checklist.confirm: That the frames resist side-to-side and front-to-back swing forces without racking, and whether corner braces are needed.
checklist.why: Swinging pushes the top of the frame back and forth; racking is not computed.

checklist.confirm: Burial depth (24"), soil, what each leg's end stands on (gravel or tamped soil), whether the backfill or concrete around it sheds water away from the wood, and lumber rated for ground contact (UC4A, or UC4B if critical or hard to replace).
checklist.why: Burial keeps the frame from lifting and walking; tipping and anchoring are not computed.

checklist.confirm: Hangers rated for swing use, installed through the beam as the manufacturer specifies, with holes no larger than the bending check takes.
checklist.why: The hanger margin uses the manufacturer's rating, which holds only for its specified installation.

checklist.confirm: Boards free of large knots near the edges (especially near midspan of the beam), steep grain slope, splits, and wane.
checklist.why: Design values assume the grade; a defect in the wrong place lowers strength more than the grade allows for.

checklist.confirm: An inspection routine: nuts and bolts twice a month, seats and chains monthly (CPSC Pub. 324, p. 5), and decay at the ground line.
checklist.why: Wood shrinks and bolts loosen, especially in pressure-treated lumber that was sold wet.

steps.title: Treat every cut with preservative

method.name: Brushed on
setup: Use the preservative on the shopping list, made for treating cuts in treated wood, and read its label for how to apply it and how long to let it dry.
technique: Brush the sawdust off each cut.
Brush the preservative onto each of the 2 cuts on the piece, and onto any corner you rounded or chamfered, until the wood stops soaking it in.
Add a second coat if the label calls for one.
Wipe off what has not soaked in.
Treat 1 this way.
mistakes: Leaving a cut bare because it will not show, such as the foot of a leg, leaves wood the treatment may never have reached. Coat every cut.
Bolting a part in place before its cuts are treated hides faces you can no longer reach. Treat every cut first.

safety.text: Read the precautions on the preservative’s label before you open it, and follow them: the label says what to wear and where to work.

steps.title: Treat every cut with preservative

method.name: Brushed on
setup: Use the preservative on the shopping list, made for treating cuts in treated wood, and read its label for how to apply it and how long to let it dry.
technique: Brush the sawdust off each cut.
Brush the preservative onto each of the 2 cuts on the piece, and onto any corner you rounded or chamfered, until the wood stops soaking it in.
Add a second coat if the label calls for one.
Wipe off what has not soaked in.
Treat 1 this way.

method.name: With a spade bit, from one side
setup: Clamp the parts together in their positions from the plan.
Chuck a 9/16" bit, for the 1/2" bolts, with an extension if the bit alone does not reach 5".
technique: Mark each hole center from the cut detail on the face you drill from.
Start the bit at low speed so its point does not wander, then drill square to the face, 5" through every part.
Back the bit out often to clear the chips. A spade bit does not pull them out on its own.
Drill 8 holes this way.
mistakes: Unclamping the parts before every hole is drilled lets them shift, so later holes do not line up. Drill all the holes in a joint before you unclamp it.
Pushing the bit out through the far face tears out the wood around the hole. Slow down as the point comes through, and finish from the far side if it splinters.

safety.text: Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.
Unplug the tool, or take out its battery, before you change a blade or bit.
Drill 9/16" for a 1/2" bolt. A hole a little larger than the bolt lets it go in without being driven.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.

checklist.element: Leg-to-beam bolt and gusset, each frame
checklist.confirm: Bolt size (1/2", 8-7/16" grip), edge and end distances in the legs and beam, washers on the tilted outer faces, and that the gusset and bolt together carry the beam's reaction.
checklist.why: Each frame carries half of every swing load into the legs through this joint; connections are not computed.

checklist.confirm: Ply bolt pattern and spacing (6 bolts entered), and that every hanger's load reaches all 2 plies.
checklist.why: The checks assume each ply carries an equal share of every load (decision 0013); that holds only if the plies are fastened together and every load reaches every ply.

checklist.confirm: That each frame holds the beam against rolling over at its support.
checklist.why: The beam stability factor assumes it; without that restraint the beam can buckle sideways at a lower load.

checklist.confirm: That the frames resist side-to-side and front-to-back swing forces without racking, and whether corner braces are needed.
checklist.why: Swinging pushes the top of the frame back and forth; racking is not computed.

checklist.confirm: Anchor type and count (1 per foot), that the rated pull-out holds in this soil, how each anchor is fastened to its leg, and how they are buried or covered.
checklist.why: The anchor check gives the pull on one anchor from the swing alone; the soil, the fastening to the leg, and sliding along the ground are not computed.

checklist.confirm: Hangers rated for swing use, installed through the beam as the manufacturer specifies, with holes no larger than the bending check takes.
checklist.why: The hanger margin uses the manufacturer's rating, which holds only for its specified installation.

checklist.confirm: Boards free of large knots near the edges (especially near midspan of the beam), steep grain slope, splits, and wane.
checklist.why: Design values assume the grade; a defect in the wrong place lowers strength more than the grade allows for.

checklist.confirm: An inspection routine: nuts and bolts twice a month, seats and chains monthly (CPSC Pub. 324, p. 5), and decay at the ground line.
checklist.why: Wood shrinks and bolts loosen, especially in pressure-treated lumber that was sold wet.

steps.title: Treat every cut with preservative

method.name: Brushed on
setup: Use the preservative on the shopping list, made for treating cuts in treated wood, and read its label for how to apply it and how long to let it dry.
technique: Brush the sawdust off each cut.
Brush the preservative onto each of the 2 cuts on the piece, and onto any corner you rounded or chamfered, until the wood stops soaking it in.
Add a second coat if the label calls for one.
Wipe off what has not soaked in.
Treat 2 this way.
mistakes: Leaving a cut bare because it will not show, such as the foot of a leg, leaves wood the treatment may never have reached. Coat every cut.
Bolting a part in place before its cuts are treated hides faces you can no longer reach. Treat every cut first.

method.name: Brushed in
setup: Use the preservative on the shopping list, made for treating cuts in treated wood, and read its label for how to apply it and how long to let it dry.
technique: Brush or blow the chips out of each hole.

Wet a brush narrow enough for a 9/16" hole, or a rag wrapped on a thin stick, with the preservative, and work it through the 3" of the hole from one face, then from the other, so the whole inside is wet.
Wipe off what runs out onto the faces.
Treat 6 holes this way, then put in the bolts once the label says it has soaked in.
mistakes: Coating only the ends of a hole leaves bare wood in the middle, where the parts meet. Work the brush through from both faces.

steps.title: Treat every cut with preservative

method.name: Brushed on
setup: Use the preservative on the shopping list, made for treating cuts in treated wood, and read its label for how to apply it and how long to let it dry.
technique: Brush the sawdust off each cut.
Brush the preservative onto each of the 2 cuts on the piece, and onto any corner you rounded or chamfered, until the wood stops soaking it in.
Add a second coat if the label calls for one.
Wipe off what has not soaked in.
Treat 2 this way.
mistakes: Leaving a cut bare because it will not show, such as the foot of a leg, leaves wood the treatment may never have reached. Coat every cut.
Bolting a part in place before its cuts are treated hides faces you can no longer reach. Treat every cut first.

steps.title: Bolt the crossbars and gussets across the legs

method.name: With a spade bit, from one side
setup: Clamp the parts together in their positions from the plan.
Chuck a 9/16" bit, for the 1/2" bolts, with an extension if the bit alone does not reach 5".
technique: Mark each hole center from the cut detail on the face you drill from.
Start the bit at low speed so its point does not wander, then drill square to the face, 5" through every part.
Back the bit out often to clear the chips. A spade bit does not pull them out on its own.
Drill 8 holes this way.
mistakes: Unclamping the parts before every hole is drilled lets them shift, so later holes do not line up. Drill all the holes in a joint before you unclamp it.
Pushing the bit out through the far face tears out the wood around the hole. Slow down as the point comes through, and finish from the far side if it splinters.

safety.text: Clamp the work down, so both hands are free for the tool.

Drill 9/16" for a 1/2" bolt. A hole a little larger than the bolt lets it go in without being driven.
Wear safety glasses or goggles while the tool runs. It can throw chips, splinters, and dust toward your face.
